title: Globular cluster NGC 4147

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows NGC 4147, a globular cluster lying about 60 000 light-years away in Coma Berenices, a northern constellation whose name means Berenice's Hair. A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical ball of old stars held together by gravity.

NGC 4147 played a part in a larger project. It was one of many globular clusters that astronomers used to work out how much mass the Milky Way holds in total. In general, the way objects orbit a galaxy depends on how much mass pulls on them, so tracking distant clusters offers a way to weigh the whole system.

Much of a galaxy's mass is thought to lie in forms that do not shine, so measurements like this rely on indirect tracers. Far-off clusters such as NGC 4147 are useful because they sample the galaxy's gravity well away from its bright center.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.45 x 3.46 arcminutes) and distance (60000 light years), the frame spans roughly 60 × 60 light-years. Its light set out about 60,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and a cluster this distant needs a powerful telescope to be seen as individual stars.

explore: The picture was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through visible and near-infrared filters. Hubble's sharp view separates the cluster's crowded stars individually, which is what makes such a distant object useful for precise measurements.
